prompt: A municipal billing service calculates each utility statement in the same steps, but each district supplies its own rate formula and may add a formula module without changing statement processing. Which design keeps those calculations independently replaceable?

options.text: Give each district rate rule the same calculation interface; let statement processing delegate that step while keeping its remaining sequence fixed.
Add a district branch inside statement processing and extend that method whenever a new formula arrives.
Make every district a separate statement-workflow subtype, duplicating the steps around its rate calculation.
Have each caller calculate its district's rate before invoking the same statement service.
Store every formula as a numeric rate table and choose rows by district, even though modules supply different algorithms.

feedback.reason: The workflow is stable, but its rate algorithm varies by district and is supplied independently. Delegate that calculation through one policy contract so a new formula does not alter statement processing.

details.mechanismOrProperty: An interchangeable policy holds one rate algorithm behind a common operation. The stable workflow selects and invokes the policy; it does not contain or reproduce each algorithm.
details.scenarioApplication: District modules provide the calculation while the statement service retains the same validation and delivery steps. That matches the stated separation between rate changes and statement processing.
details.errorCorrection: A branch in statement processing is the closest simple alternative, but every new module would still require changing that workflow. The scenario explicitly rules out that coupling.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A short conditional can be clearer when the alternatives are few and change together with the workflow. Separate policies pay off here because district rules arrive independently.
details.transfer: Separate a variable algorithm from its caller when the caller's sequence remains stable and the alternatives must evolve independently.

messages.text: That keeps the changing formulas inside the workflow the prompt says must remain untouched when a district adds a module.
The workflow is shared; a subtype per formula couples unrelated processing to each district's calculation and makes the common sequence drift.
This moves formula selection and implementation to callers, so two callers can apply different rules for the same district.
The scenario varies executable calculation rules, not only numeric values; a row lookup cannot represent those different algorithms by itself.

prompt: A claims desk follows one intake and review sequence. Regional eligibility formulas are issued by different underwriting groups, and a formula can be replaced without changing how a claim moves through the desk. Where should the varying rule live?

options.text: Represent each regional eligibility algorithm behind the same policy operation and have the stable claim review delegate its decision to the selected one.
Add regional conditions to the intake service and let its review sequence grow with each underwriting formula.
Create a separate intake-and-review workflow class for every underwriting group.
Ask each claims clerk to select and apply a formula manually before starting review.
Convert every eligibility algorithm into a fixed list of region thresholds even when the groups supply different computations.

feedback.reason: Eligibility behavior changes by region, but claim review does not. Put each algorithm behind one policy contract and make the unchanged review path call the selected policy.

details.mechanismOrProperty: The policy object encapsulates a replaceable calculation. The caller depends on the shared operation rather than branching on each underwriting group's implementation.
details.scenarioApplication: The selected regional rule decides eligibility inside the existing claim sequence; intake, evidence collection, and review remain shared across groups.
details.errorCorrection: A regional branch appears direct, but it puts every independent formula change into the shared intake path. That contradicts the premise that underwriting groups replace formulas without editing claim flow.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: One formula with a few numeric parameters may remain a single calculation. Separate implementations fit when the algorithm itself varies independently.
details.transfer: Keep a caller stable by delegating one independently varying algorithm through a common contract.

messages.text: That makes the common claim path own rules that the groups replace independently, contrary to the stated change boundary.
This duplicates the shared claim lifecycle even though only eligibility calculation varies.
The same region could be treated differently by different clerks; the rule needs one selected implementation, not caller discipline.
The stated variation is in algorithms, not merely threshold values, so a fixed threshold table cannot express every supplied rule.

prompt: A lending platform uses the same repayment posting steps for every loan. At the time of posting, the account's plan selects one of several allocation algorithms, and finance can add a plan without modifying the posting service. Which boundary best supports that change?

options.text: Give allocation algorithms a shared operation and let the posting service invoke the account's selected policy without embedding the algorithms in posting.
Branch inside posting on each plan name and revise the service whenever finance adds another plan.
Use a subclass of the posting service for each plan and duplicate the posting steps around allocation.
Pass the plan name to each caller and require every caller to implement its own allocation switch.
Add a global mutable current-plan variable that each allocation changes before posting starts.

feedback.reason: The algorithm belongs to the account's plan and can vary at runtime, while posting stays the same. Delegate allocation to the selected policy rather than expanding the posting service.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A policy interface makes the allocation algorithm interchangeable. The service controls the stable posting operation and supplies the account-specific policy for that request.
details.scenarioApplication: Each account's selected allocation rule is used during its own posting flow. No process-wide plan variable or per-caller duplicate switch is needed.
details.errorCorrection: The posting branch is the closest alternative, but it couples each new finance plan to the service. The case specifically requires adding plans without editing that service.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If selection were fixed at deployment and algorithms were simple, a small branch might remain reasonable. Runtime account-specific selection makes an independent policy boundary useful here.
details.transfer: When one request chooses among independently varying algorithms, pass that request's policy into the stable operation instead of storing selection globally.

messages.text: The new plan would require changing the very posting service the prompt says finance must leave unchanged.
Plan choice changes allocation, not the common posting lifecycle; duplicating that lifecycle creates avoidable divergence.
Different callers could allocate the same account differently because the selection rule is copied outside the posting service.
Concurrent accounts could overwrite that shared value and use the wrong allocation rule; the policy must be selected per account/request.

prompt: A concert venue keeps one seat-allocation workflow. A promoter may choose among independently maintained pricing algorithms for each event; adding a new algorithm must not change seat assignment or ticket delivery. How should pricing fit into the workflow?

options.text: Expose one pricing operation and supply the event's selected algorithm to the unchanged seat-allocation workflow.
Add promoter-specific pricing cases to seat allocation and let those cases decide delivery details too.
Build a full seat-allocation subclass for each promoter's pricing algorithm.
Let each ticket-delivery caller calculate prices using its own promoter check.
Store a single scalar multiplier and apply it to every promoter, ignoring their separately maintained algorithms.

feedback.reason: The event selects the price algorithm, while seat allocation and delivery are stable. Keeping pricing behind one operation lets promoters vary that behavior without spreading checks through the workflow.

details.mechanismOrProperty: An interchangeable pricing policy contains the event's algorithm. The workflow asks that policy for a result and continues with its unchanged allocation and delivery steps.
details.scenarioApplication: Promoter-specific computation changes per event; seat assignment and ticket delivery do not. The policy boundary isolates exactly that variable part.
details.errorCorrection: A subclass per promoter is the nearest structural alternative, but it carries unchanged seating and delivery behavior into each variant. Only price computation differs.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Configuration data is enough when every option uses the same computation with different values. Separate policies fit when the calculation itself is maintained independently.
details.transfer: Isolate only the behavior that varies; keep the shared workflow outside the policy.

messages.text: That couples pricing to unrelated allocation and delivery behavior despite the stated requirement that both remain unchanged.
A promoter changes pricing only; duplicating seating and delivery flow adds behavior the scenario says is common.
Delivery callers would own duplicated price logic and could disagree for the same event.
A multiplier cannot stand in for the distinct pricing algorithms the promoters maintain and select.

prompt: A captioning studio keeps one ingest and display pipeline. Each customer can select a speech-recognition engine, and the studio can add another engine while preserving the pipeline's timing and error contract. What should the pipeline depend on?

options.text: Make recognition a common operation with a customer-selected engine policy; keep the ingest and display pipeline independent of engine details.
Add a customer-and-engine switch to the display pipeline and extend it for each new recognizer.
Create a separate ingest, recognition, and display class for every recognizer.
Let each display client call its preferred recognizer directly before rendering captions.
Use a shared mutable recognizer field that every customer request replaces before the pipeline starts.

feedback.reason: Recognition is the independently selected algorithm; ingest and display stay fixed. The pipeline should invoke a policy for recognition without learning each engine's implementation.

details.mechanismOrProperty: The shared recognition contract is implemented by interchangeable engines. A request carries the selected implementation through the unchanged pipeline.
details.scenarioApplication: Customer-specific engine choice is scoped to each caption stream, while the timing and error contract remains controlled by the common pipeline.
details.errorCorrection: A recognizer branch in the pipeline may appear straightforward, but every added engine would modify that pipeline and expose its internals to another variation.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If several engines must run together and their results be combined, the problem becomes composition/aggregation. This case selects one engine per customer stream.
details.transfer: Use a request-scoped interchangeable algorithm when each caller chooses one behavior but the surrounding process stays common.

messages.text: This leaks engine selection into a pipeline whose timing and behavior must remain stable as engines are added.
Only recognition varies; copying the unchanged ingest and display steps makes those common contracts drift.
Recognition choice and error behavior would be duplicated across display clients rather than governed by the customer selection.
Overlapping requests could replace one another's engine; the selected policy must belong to the customer request, not shared mutable state.

prompt: An energy exchange runs the same discharge-reservation steps for every meter. Each grid operator supplies a different priority algorithm, and a new algorithm can be installed independently of reservation processing. Where should priority calculation occur?

options.text: Delegate priority calculation through one policy operation selected for the meter; leave the discharge-reservation steps in the shared service.
Add every operator's priority rule to the reservation service's branch logic.
Give every operator a complete reservation-service subclass containing its priority rule.
Ask meter callers to compute priority and pass the ordered meters to the service.
Represent every operator's algorithm as one fixed priority number stored on the meter.

feedback.reason: Priority is a replaceable algorithm, not part of the reservation sequence. Selecting the meter's policy and delegating that calculation isolates operator changes from shared reservation behavior.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A policy contract exposes the priority calculation and allows separate implementations. The workflow uses one selected policy without branching on operator internals.
details.scenarioApplication: The selected operator's algorithm ranks the current meter candidates; reservation validation and commit remain the same for every operator.
details.errorCorrection: Putting all rules in the reservation service is the closest simple approach, but it turns every operator addition into a change to the shared workflow.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: When the differences are only data values, store those values and keep one formula. Here each operator supplies a different ranking algorithm.
details.transfer: Delegate a changing algorithm through a stable operation rather than branching the workflow that surrounds it.

messages.text: That makes installing an independent algorithm require edits to the shared reservation sequence.
This duplicates capacity checks and reservation steps that are common across operators.
Callers would reproduce operator-specific algorithms, so the same meter could be ranked differently by different callers.
The premise varies the algorithm itself; a fixed number cannot express how the different rules rank candidate meters.

prompt: A loyalty platform follows one purchase-crediting sequence. The campaign attached to a purchase chooses among distinct points formulas, and campaign owners can replace formulas without changing how purchases are recorded. What is the cleanest calculation boundary?

options.text: Have the campaign supply a points policy behind a shared calculation contract; let purchase crediting call it and keep recording common.
Add a campaign switch to purchase recording and update it for every new points formula.
Subclass the purchase-recording service for every campaign and duplicate the recording steps.
Make every purchase caller calculate points using its own copy of the campaign rules.
Ask a central mutable singleton to switch its current formula between purchases.

feedback.reason: The campaign chooses a formula, while purchase recording is shared. A policy keeps each executable calculation independent and lets the common sequence delegate points computation.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A campaign-specific strategy implements one calculation contract. The purchase workflow supplies or resolves that strategy for the current purchase and continues unchanged.
details.scenarioApplication: Each purchase uses the formula selected by its campaign, without adding campaign-specific calculations to the code that records purchases.
details.errorCorrection: Caller-side calculation is plausible, but it distributes campaign rules among clients and makes consistent updates harder than one selected policy implementation.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: One formula with campaign-specific parameters may not need separate implementations. Use separate policies when the computation itself changes.
details.transfer: Keep common transaction steps stable and inject the independently selected algorithm at its calculation seam.

messages.text: The shared recording sequence would have to change whenever a campaign replaces its formula.
Campaigns vary points calculation, not purchase recording; duplicating that stable work creates unnecessary coupling.
Copied rules can diverge across callers, even for purchases belonging to the same campaign.
Concurrent purchases can observe another campaign's selected formula; the policy must be selected with each purchase.

prompt: A delivery service performs one dispatch workflow. A route plan selects a different stop-ranking algorithm for each contract, and planners can add algorithms without changing dispatch. Which structure fits this split?

options.text: Place stop ranking behind a shared policy operation and let the route plan select it before the unchanged dispatch workflow uses it.
Put route-plan conditions in dispatch and add ranking logic there whenever planners add an algorithm.
Create a separate dispatch workflow for each route plan and repeat loading, validation, and sending steps.
Have each planner client rank stops and send the resulting route to dispatch.
Store the current route plan in a process-wide field and let a single ranker read it.

feedback.reason: Route plans change stop ranking independently, while dispatch is common. A selected ranking policy isolates the variable computation from dispatch control flow.

details.mechanismOrProperty: One policy operation represents stop ranking; each route plan supplies an implementation, and dispatch depends only on that contract.
details.scenarioApplication: The service executes the same dispatch sequence after asking the route's selected algorithm to rank its stops.
details.errorCorrection: A process-wide selection looks reusable, but simultaneous contracts can overwrite one another's choice. The route-specific policy belongs to the current dispatch.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A single ranker with adjustable values is simpler when only the data changes. Independently supplied algorithms need the separate behavior boundary described here.
details.transfer: Bind interchangeable behavior to the work item or request that selects it, not to global mutable configuration.

messages.text: That couples algorithm additions to the shared dispatch steps, which the scenario requires to stay unchanged.
The route plans vary only in ranking; duplicated dispatch steps can diverge for no stated reason.
This spreads contract-specific algorithms across clients instead of letting one plan select its calculation.
Concurrent dispatches can read a different contract's plan; selection must be scoped to the route being dispatched.

prompt: A museum donation system uses one receipt workflow. Each campaign may select a different fee calculation, and finance maintains those calculations separately from receipt formatting and delivery. Where should the fee variation sit?

options.text: Let each campaign provide a fee policy behind one calculation operation; the receipt workflow invokes it without owning campaign formulas.
Add campaign-specific fee branches to the receipt workflow and edit that workflow when a formula changes.
Make a receipt-workflow subclass for every campaign and duplicate its formatting and delivery steps.
Require each donation form to compute its own campaign fee before sending receipt data.
Store all campaigns as a single hard-coded percentage, even where finance supplies different formulas.

feedback.reason: Fee behavior varies independently from the receipt lifecycle. The workflow should invoke the campaign's calculation policy rather than embedding formulas or sending them to forms.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A shared calculation contract separates the chosen fee algorithm from the process that creates and delivers receipts.
details.scenarioApplication: Finance can update one campaign's policy without changing the receipt workflow or each donation form.
details.errorCorrection: A formula in the form is the nearest alternative, but it creates multiple finance-rule owners. Keeping selection in the campaign policy preserves one calculation boundary.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If fees differ only by a scalar rate, configuration can be simpler. Use distinct policies when the formulas themselves are different.
details.transfer: Place independently maintained calculations behind a shared operation and keep presentation/process steps outside them.

messages.text: This couples calculation maintenance to receipt formatting and delivery, despite their stated independence.
Campaigns vary the fee calculation only; copying the receipt lifecycle adds unrelated changes to each variant.
Each form becomes a second owner of finance logic and can calculate the same campaign fee differently.
A percentage parameter cannot represent the distinct calculations finance maintains for those campaigns.

prompt: A transit planner uses one trip-search sequence. Each agency chooses its own accessibility preference algorithm, while result rendering and fare lookup stay common. Which decision keeps those responsibilities apart?

options.text: Give accessibility ranking one policy contract selected by agency; leave search, rendering, and fare lookup in their common workflow.
Add each agency's preference rules to the rendering layer and let it rank the results.
Build an agency-specific trip-search class that repeats result retrieval, rendering, and fare lookup.
Let each caller reorder results after the planner returns them, using copied agency rules.
Use a mutable active-agency setting shared by all concurrent trip searches.

feedback.reason: Agency choice affects ranking only; the rest of trip search stays common. Isolate that algorithm behind a policy instead of extending search or display logic.

details.mechanismOrProperty: The planner delegates ranking to the selected policy and continues to use its shared search and rendering operations.
details.scenarioApplication: The selected agency's accessibility ranking shapes the results, while fare lookup and rendering do not need to know how ranking works.
details.errorCorrection: Caller-side reordering is plausible, but copied rules are hard to keep consistent and bypass the planner's agency selection.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If every agency uses the same algorithm with different weights, one configurable ranker may suffice; separate algorithms justify separate policies.
details.transfer: Keep a variable decision rule separate from stable retrieval and presentation steps.

messages.text: Rendering is common and does not own the agency-specific ranking calculation; this mixes display with selection.
Only ranking varies, so duplicating the entire trip workflow couples unrelated responsibilities to agency choice.
Copied caller logic can disagree and leaves the planner's selected agency policy unenforced.
One search could change the agency used by another; each request needs its own selected policy.

prompt: A game studio runs the same reward-settlement steps for every season. Season designers supply distinct scoring formulas that may be replaced between seasons without changing settlement. How should settlement obtain a score?

options.text: Use a common score-policy contract selected for the season, and let settlement delegate scoring before applying its shared reward steps.
Add season-specific scoring branches throughout the settlement service.
Create a separate settlement subclass per season and copy the shared reward steps into each one.
Ask each client to compute points and send the resulting total to settlement.
Store the currently active season in a mutable singleton read during settlement.

feedback.reason: The season selects an independently maintained scoring algorithm; the reward steps are stable. A policy keeps those changes outside settlement while preserving one score operation.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Each season supplies a compatible scoring policy. Settlement invokes that policy for the current season and retains ownership of the common reward sequence.
details.scenarioApplication: Scoring can change between seasons without rewriting reward settlement or relying on every client to compute points correctly.
details.errorCorrection: A client-calculated total is the nearest alternative, but it duplicates the season rule outside the selected owner and lets clients disagree.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: One formula with season-specific weights is often easier to configure. Separate algorithms are warranted when designers replace the computation itself.
details.transfer: When an independently selected algorithm feeds a stable workflow, give it a shared contract and keep selection local to the request.

messages.text: This spreads formula changes into the common reward process, although designers replace scoring independently.
Only scoring varies; copying reward settlement makes common behavior vulnerable to season-specific drift.
Each client would own a copy of season scoring and could submit a total that disagrees with the selected season rule.
Concurrent settlements for different seasons could read the wrong active value; selection must accompany the season's operation.

prompt: A support desk follows the same ticket-triage sequence for every account. Account plans provide separate urgency-ranking rules, and plan owners can add a rule without changing triage. What belongs at the ranking seam?

options.text: Define one urgency-ranking operation and let the account plan provide its implementation to the unchanged triage sequence.
Put plan-specific branches in triage and extend the sequence when a plan owner adds a rule.
Create a complete triage workflow subclass for each account plan.
Let each ticket intake client rank urgency using its own plan checks.
Have every plan mutate a shared ranker before its ticket is triaged.

feedback.reason: The triage sequence is shared and account plans select distinct ranking rules. A policy object makes the ranking replaceable without plan branches in triage.

details.mechanismOrProperty: The stable workflow asks one ranking contract to order the ticket. The account's policy implements that contract for its plan.
details.scenarioApplication: Plan owners can add rankings independently while ticket intake, assignment, and notification retain their common sequence.
details.errorCorrection: A plan-specific workflow is a plausible separation, but it duplicates all triage steps even though only ranking changes.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the plan set is fixed and ranking is a short stable condition, a local branch can be easier to maintain. Here additions must not edit triage.
details.transfer: Extract the single algorithm that changes independently; do not fork an otherwise shared workflow.

messages.text: That requires changing triage for every plan addition, contrary to the fixed workflow premise.
Plan rules alter ranking only; duplicating intake and assignment steps adds needless plan-specific workflows.
Different clients could apply different rankings to the same account plan because the algorithm is duplicated.
Concurrent ticket intake can change the shared ranker between selection and use; the plan policy must be request-scoped.

prompt: A document review service keeps one intake and redaction workflow. Each client selects a different redaction rule set whose executable logic is maintained by that client's compliance team. Which design isolates those changes?

options.text: Expose one redaction operation and let the selected client policy implement it; keep intake and orchestration in the shared service.
Embed every client's redaction conditions in intake and change that workflow for each compliance update.
Create a separate intake service for each client and duplicate document handling around its rule set.
Let client-facing screens redact documents before sending them to the service.
Treat every executable policy as a static set of terms and ignore the teams' distinct rule logic.

feedback.reason: Client compliance logic varies independently from document intake. Keep one redaction contract in the workflow and select the client's policy implementation for that operation.

details.mechanismOrProperty: An interchangeable policy encapsulates the client's algorithm; the service depends on its operation rather than each compliance team's internal rules.
details.scenarioApplication: The selected policy redacts the document while the existing service continues its common intake and orchestration steps.
details.errorCorrection: A list of terms would be a reasonable configuration model for literal substitutions. It cannot express the executable logic described in this case.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: For simple data-only variation, avoid adding separate implementations. Use a policy boundary when independently maintained behavior, not just values, varies.
details.transfer: Separate client-owned algorithms from shared processing when the rules are executable and independently maintained.

messages.text: This couples compliance-team algorithm changes to shared intake, even though the teams maintain those rules separately.
Only redaction behavior differs; duplicating shared document handling is broader than the stated variation.
The screens are not the owners of independently maintained compliance logic, so they can diverge from one another.
The premise says the client-specific rule sets contain different executable logic, not merely different literal terms.

prompt: A regional clinic schedules appointments through one booking sequence. Each clinic supplies a different slot-ranking algorithm, while confirmation and patient-record updates stay identical. How should booking apply the selected ranking?

options.text: Call one slot-ranking contract implemented by the selected clinic policy, then continue the same booking and confirmation sequence.
Put each clinic's slot algorithm inside the booking sequence and update it when a clinic changes its ranking.
Create one complete booking workflow subclass per clinic, duplicating confirmation and record updates.
Let each calendar client rank clinic slots with a local copy of the algorithm.
Set the active clinic in a shared singleton and let the ranker read that value later.

feedback.reason: Slot ranking is the only clinic-specific behavior. Booking should delegate that algorithm and continue with its common confirmation and record updates.

details.mechanismOrProperty: One policy operation represents ranking, and each clinic provides a compatible implementation selected for its booking request.
details.scenarioApplication: The clinic-specific ranker chooses slots without making confirmation or patient-record code depend on clinic algorithms.
details.errorCorrection: A singleton selection looks like a convenient place to choose a clinic, but it can be changed by another concurrent booking. Keep the policy attached to the request.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: One shared ranker with data parameters is simpler for small numeric differences. Independent clinic algorithms need a replaceable implementation seam.
details.transfer: Pass behavior selection with the operation that uses it; avoid mutable global selectors for concurrent work.

messages.text: That makes clinic algorithm maintenance a change to the shared booking flow, contrary to the separation in the stem.
Those steps are explicitly identical; the subclass copies behavior unrelated to slot ranking.
Client copies can disagree and create a booking order that does not match the clinic's selected rule.
A concurrent booking can overwrite the clinic selection between setup and ranking, causing the wrong policy to run.

prompt: An online shop uses one checkout sequence. Each seller program supplies its own return-fee calculation, and adding a program must not change payment capture or receipt creation. Which design keeps the variation local?

options.text: Let each seller program provide a fee policy through one operation, called by checkout without altering payment capture or receipt creation.
Add seller-specific fee cases to checkout and change its payment and receipt path for each program.
Create a full checkout subtype per seller program and copy payment and receipt handling into it.
Make each seller's storefront calculate the fee and pass the number to payment capture.
Use one fixed percentage for every seller even though each program maintains a different calculation.

feedback.reason: Only return-fee calculation varies by seller program. Keep that algorithm behind a policy operation and leave checkout's payment and receipt sequence shared.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A selected fee policy implements one calculation contract. The checkout flow invokes it without embedding seller-specific formulas.
details.scenarioApplication: Each return uses the applicable seller's fee rule while payment capture and receipt creation retain their existing behavior.
details.errorCorrection: Storefront calculation is the nearest alternative, but it duplicates policy ownership across clients. Checkout should select one policy for the seller program.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A single formula with different rates can be parameterized. Separate strategies fit independently maintained calculations, as stated here.
details.transfer: Place a variable algorithm at one explicit seam rather than copying it into every caller or surrounding workflow.

messages.text: This spreads a return-fee variation into the shared payment and receipt operations the scenario keeps unchanged.
Seller programs differ in fee calculation only; copied payment and receipt code creates unnecessary divergence.
Storefronts become separate owners of finance rules and could submit inconsistent fees for the same program.
A single percentage cannot represent the independently maintained formulas the seller programs provide.

prompt: A content moderation service runs the same submission workflow for every community. Each community chooses a different scoring algorithm maintained by its moderators; adding one cannot require an edit to submission processing. What should processing invoke?

options.text: Invoke the community's selected scoring policy through a shared operation while leaving submission processing common.
Add moderator-specific scoring conditions to submission processing and edit it whenever a community adds a rule.
Make a submission-workflow subclass for each community and duplicate validation and storage steps.
Let each community client score submissions and send only the resulting value to the service.
Put all moderator rules in one fixed threshold table even though their algorithms differ.

feedback.reason: The community owns a replaceable scoring algorithm; the service owns the common submission sequence. Processing should delegate scoring through a shared policy operation.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A strategy encapsulates each scoring algorithm behind a common contract. The workflow selects the community policy and invokes it without branching on its internals.
details.scenarioApplication: Moderators can maintain their own scoring behavior without changing validation or storage in submission processing.
details.errorCorrection: A threshold table is appropriate for data-only differences. It falls short because this scenario explicitly varies executable scoring rules.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If one algorithm remains stable and communities only configure values, prefer the simpler parameterized calculation. Separate policies are for algorithmic variation.
details.transfer: Distinguish data variation from algorithm variation before choosing configuration or interchangeable implementations.

messages.text: This makes a moderator's independent algorithm addition a change to the shared submission path.
Community scoring is the varying behavior; duplicating common validation and storage does not isolate it.
Scoring logic would be distributed among clients and could vary by caller for the same community.
Threshold data cannot represent different scoring algorithms when the rules themselves change structurally.

prompt: A repair shop uses one work-order flow. Each service contract supplies a different labor-estimate algorithm, and contract owners can replace those algorithms without changing diagnosis, approval, or invoice steps. Which part should vary independently?

options.text: Give labor estimation a shared policy contract with one implementation per contract, then continue the unchanged work-order steps.
Add contract-specific estimate branches through diagnosis and approval, then edit those steps for every new contract.
Create a complete work-order subclass for each contract and copy diagnosis, approval, and invoicing behavior.
Let each invoice screen recompute labor with its own copy of the contract rules.
Represent every contract's independent algorithm as a single hourly-rate field.

feedback.reason: The contract changes the estimation algorithm, not the work-order sequence. Delegating estimation through a policy keeps diagnosis, approval, and invoicing common.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A contract-specific policy implements labor estimation behind one operation. The service invokes it at the estimate step and owns the surrounding flow.
details.scenarioApplication: Contract owners can update an estimate algorithm without changing diagnosis, approval, or invoice behavior.
details.errorCorrection: A rate parameter is the nearest simpler model, but the premise varies the algorithm rather than a single hourly value.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: When only rates or constants differ, configure one calculation. When contracts replace executable rules independently, isolate those implementations.
details.transfer: Use a shared policy contract for independently replaceable business algorithms; keep adjacent stable steps in the workflow.

messages.text: This carries estimate variation into diagnosis and approval, even though the prompt states those work-order steps are common.
Only labor estimation changes; copying the rest of the work-order flow creates separate versions of shared behavior.
The same work order could receive different estimates from different screens because the rule is duplicated at presentation clients.
A rate field fits a shared formula, but it cannot express the different estimate algorithms specified here.

prompt: A regional food cooperative uses one delivery-planning sequence. Each region supplies its own cold-chain priority algorithm, and planners can add a region without changing dispatch or proof-of-delivery steps. Where should ranking be selected?

options.text: Let each region supply a ranking policy through the same operation and select it for a plan before common dispatch continues.
Add regional priority branches to dispatch and extend its control flow when a region is introduced.
Create one full delivery plan class per region and repeat dispatch and proof-of-delivery behavior.
Ask each warehouse client to rank deliveries using its own region rule before submitting the plan.
Change a shared active-region value before each planner call and have dispatch read it later.

feedback.reason: The region selects a priority algorithm and dispatch remains fixed. A plan-scoped policy keeps the ranking replaceable without branching the delivery sequence.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A common ranking operation separates region-specific computation from dispatch. The selected implementation travels with the plan that uses it.
details.scenarioApplication: The region's algorithm ranks items, after which the common dispatch and proof-of-delivery operations proceed as before.
details.errorCorrection: A shared active-region setting is unsafe for overlapping plan builds because one plan can change another's selection.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: When a few values differ, parameterize one ranker. Independently supplied algorithms need distinct policy implementations.
details.transfer: Scope algorithm selection to the plan or request that consumes it, not a mutable process-wide setting.

messages.text: This makes regional algorithm changes edit dispatch, contradicting the independently addable region requirement.
The regions differ in ranking only; copying dispatch and proof-of-delivery is unrelated to that decision.
This duplicates the region algorithm among warehouse clients and can produce inconsistent rankings.
Parallel plan generation could overwrite that shared selection; the policy must be associated with its particular plan.
